17:73.heading: Ayah 73

blocks.text: They were about to tempt you away from what We have revealed to you [O Prophet] so that you would fabricate something else and attribute it to Us; then they would have surely taken you as a close friend.

This verse shows that the central struggle with those who uphold falsehood is not over some peripheral aspect of religion, but over revelation itself. They want the bearer of the message to turn away from some of what has been revealed to him, even by a small change of wording, so that he attributes to Allah something Allah has not sent down. The words “They were about to tempt you away from what We have revealed to you” mean that they went to great lengths in their attempts and came close to their aim, but Allah protected His Prophet, and the revelation was not changed.

blocks.text: Pressure does not always take the form of violence. It can come through expressions of esteem, friendly treatment, and offers of reconciliation, until the price becomes a small concession. Hence the promise described in the verse: “then they would have surely taken you as a close friend.” They are willing to restore closeness and acceptance if the parts of revelation that trouble them are set aside. Acceptance by those who uphold falsehood is therefore no measure of whether a call to faith is sound; at times, it may be a sign that part of the message has been left unspoken.

17:74.heading: Ayah 74

blocks.text: Had We not made you stand firm, you would nearly have inclined to them a little.

The verse explicitly attributes deliverance to Allah’s strengthening: “Had We not made you stand firm”. If the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), despite his perfection, needed his Lord to keep him firm, then someone working to serve the faith cannot rely on intelligence, experience, or strength of character alone. Their attempt to sway him is likened to a storm that seeks to uproot a person; steadfastness is what holds that person in place.

17:75.heading: Ayah 75

blocks.text: In that case, We would have made you taste double punishment, both in this life and after death. Thereupon you would have found no helper against Us.

Because the concession being sought concerned revelation, the warning was severe: had he given way, the punishment would have been doubled in this life and after death, with no one able to help against Allah’s judgement. One lesson drawn in the commentary is that the punishment reflects the aim behind the act. Someone who imagines that surrendering part of the truth will bring strength or acceptance may find humiliation and disgrace instead of honour, because the very source of that strength is the revelation they have surrendered. The message is not protected by softening it to please people, but by preserving it as it was revealed. The more a person is entrusted with the faith, the more dangerous it becomes to tamper with it.

17:76.heading: Ayah 76

blocks.text: They were about to provoke you so as to drive you out of the land [of Makkah], but then they would not have remained after you, except for a little while[67].

After the attempt to win concessions through gentle treatment comes another method: provocation and pressure intended to drive the Messenger out of the land. The commentary presents the view that Quraysh did not succeed in forcing him out before permission came to him. He left when Allah commanded him to leave, just as Moses departed with his people when the command came, not when Pharaoh wished.

Haste can turn an action that is sound in itself into a response to an opponent’s plan.

17:77.heading: Ayah 77

blocks.text: Such was Our way with the messengers We sent before you, and you will find no change in Our way.

What the Messenger faces is not an isolated event. It is a pattern repeated in the path of the messengers: pressure to change the truth, followed by pressure to expel its bearer. The commentary also describes a pattern in Allah’s dealings: when those who uphold falsehood exhaust their efforts to mislead and expel, while the Messenger remains faithful to revelation, victory comes. Steadfastness does not mean that pressure will never reach its height. It means recognising that this stage, too, belongs to the patterns of the path, rather than treating its severity as proof that the way being followed is wrong. The words “you will find no change in Our way” keep the heart from reading every crisis as the end of the message. A crisis may be the stage just before a turning point.

17:78.heading: Ayah 78

blocks.text: Establish prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night, and the recitation of dawn [prayer][68], for the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed [by the angels][69].

After the attempts to sway and provoke him, the verses show a practical path to steadfastness: prayer. It is as though the appointed times of prayer stretch across the whole day to keep the heart connected to Allah amid the storms, so that steadfastness rests on more than psychological strength. The verse then singles out “the recitation of dawn [prayer]”. The believer begins the day with the very Quran from which those who uphold falsehood want to turn him away, renewing his direction each morning before entering the bustle of the day.

17:79.heading: Ayah 79

blocks.text: And wake up during the night and pray, as an additional prayer for you [O Prophet], so your Lord may raise you to a praised status[70].

[The Arabic word tahajjud is related to hujūd, meaning sleep. Here it evokes a worshipper casting sleep aside to stand in prayer, reciting the Quran.] The image also points to the heart: heedlessness is not overcome by spiritual sleep, but by prayer that awakens it. The commentary links this night prayer with “a praised status”, explained as the intercession promised specifically to the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him).

The verses that reach the heart in the stillness of the night correct its outlook and put its fears and hopes in order before it faces the pressures of people during the day.

17:80.heading: Ayah 80

blocks.text: And say, “My Lord, make me enter an honorable entrance[71] and make me exit an honorable exit[72], and grant me from Yourself a supporting authority.”

After warning the Messenger against entering into their compromises or leaving in response to their provocation, the verses give a supplication to guide every step: to enter truthfully and to leave truthfully. In other words, one does not enter merely because a place is safe or people approve, nor leave simply because pressure has increased. Each step should be sincerely directed towards what Allah wants, at a time that pleases Him. The commentary connects this with the departure of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) from Makkah: his delay was not merely attachment to the place; he had not yet been given permission. When permission came, he left. He then asks for “a supporting authority”: strength from Allah that supports the faith, rather than merely securing a personal gain.

17:81.heading: Ayah 81

blocks.text: And say, “The truth has come and falsehood has perished. Indeed, falsehood is bound to perish[73].”

This verse was revealed at a time when outward victory was not yet complete, yet it declares: “The truth has come and falsehood has perished.” One reflection drawn from this is that the arrival of truth begins with its bearer’s own steadfastness: resisting attempts to turn him away from revelation and provocations that would lead to a wrong decision. That itself is a victory for the truth.

blocks.text: Truth draws its strength from within, because it is revelation from Allah. Much of falsehood’s strength, by contrast, depends on circumstances and external power, both of which change. Surrendering part of revelation in pursuit of strength therefore costs a believer part of the true source of that strength. As long as the believer remains firm upon the truth, falsehood, however firmly established it may appear, carries within itself the possibility of passing away.
